body.p: I. Introduction

With the addition of claims 14-17, claims 1-17 are pending in the present application. No new matter has been added. In view of the foregoing amendments and the following remarks, it is respectfully submitted that all the pending claims are allowable, and reconsideration is respectfully requested.
Applicant notes with appreciation the acknowledgement of the claim for foreign priority and the indication that all certified copies of the priority documents have been received.
Applicant thanks the Examiner for considering the previously filed Information Disclosure Statement and the references cited therein.
II. Rejection of Claims 1 and 7-13 Under 35 U.S.C. k 102

Claims 1 and 7-13 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as anticipated by U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2013/0018526 ("Kelly"). Kelly does not anticipate any of the present claims, and the rejection should be withdrawn, for at least the following reasons.

Independent claims 1, 12, and 13 are directed to an ego vehicle (first vehicle) detecting information about a leading vehicle (second vehicle), by which the ego vehicle determines a maneuver performed by the leading vehicle or that the leading vehicle has driven over an obstacle. The ego vehicle then uses that information regarding the leading vehicle to detect the obstacle itself. Kelly does not suggest these features of an indirect detection of an obstacle by using a detection about a leading vehicle in order to detect the obstacle.

Kelly describes a special system used for developing a crash avoidance system of an ego/host vehicle 650. The special system takes the form of a dynamic motion element (DME) 100 which is a very low profile self-driving system that the ego/host vehicle 650 can drive over. The DME 100 is placed under a soft vehicle 600, referred to as a guided soft target (GST). This appears to essentially be a blow-up toy of typical car size that rides on top of the DME 100. The purpose of this combined system 100/600 is for it to simulate scenarios of a real-world vehicle while the ego/host vehicle 650 drives behind the simulation vehicle 100/600. Figs. 6A-6D show the ego/host vehicle 650 driving and crashing into the combined system 100/600. (Kelly also describes a similar system for simulating a pedestrian as shown in Fig. 7, where a soft mannequin 700 is placed on top of the DME 100.)
The Office Action cites to pars. 2, 34, 45, and 58 of Kelly, as well as Figs. 6C- 6D. Par. 2 states that the ego/host vehicle 650 can detect its surroundings using various sensors.

Par. 34 discloses using those sensors to detect presence of an obstacle in front of the ego/host vehicle 650, in order to perform a reactionary action in case an obstacle is detected with which the ego/host vehicle 650 determines it is likely to collide. Par. 34 states that some of these sensor systems are so sensitive that they may take a reactionary action even when detecting the low profile DME 100. But this is not desirable. In other words, when performing testing, we do not want the DME 100 to be treated as an obstacle. Therefore, par. 34 states that it is important to minimize an extent to which the DME 100 contributes to a detected radar (or other sensor) signature. Therefore, this section is describing ensuring that the DME 100 is not detected by the ego/host vehicle 650.

Par. 45 generally lists functions that the DME 100 can perform, including guidance/navigation and "data input and output," where inputs can include GOS information, compass information, and yaw rate information.

Par. 58 describes a use case of the simulation vehicle 100/600 forming a guided soft target system (GST) 800 to evaluate a collision mitigation system (A-CMBS) of the ego/host vehicle 650 which is supposed to take a reactionary action to a case in which, when properly functioning, the A-CMBS should detect that a collision is likely.
Thus, none of the cited sections suggest an indirect obstacle detection to which the present claims are directed.
Kelly therefore does not disclose or suggest all of the features of claims 1, 12, or 13 and therefore does not anticipate any of claims 1, 12, and 13 or any of claims 7-11, which depend from claim 1.
Withdrawal of the anticipation rejection of claims 1 and 7-13 is therefore respectfully requested.
III. Rejection of Claims 2 and 4 Under 35 U.S.C. # 103

Claims 2 and 4 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2020/0255013 ("Lee"). Claims 2 and 4 depend from claim 1 and are therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Lee merely generally describes sensors that an ego/host vehicle can use to detect presence, location, speed, direction, and type of a surrounding vehicle and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claims 1 and 7-13 is therefore respectfully requested.
IV. Rejection of Claim 3 Under 35 U.S.C. 103

Claim 3 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly, Lee, and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2005/0169530 ("Nakai"). Claim 3 depends from claim 2 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 2 because Nakai merely describes detections by an ego/host vehicle of measurements directly of the obstacle itself based on relationships between image data captured by two different cameras of the ego/host vehicle and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly and Lee noted above as to claim 2. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 3 is therefore respectfully requested.
V. Rejection of Claim 5 Under 35 U.S.C. 4 103

Claim 5 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2021/0129750 ("Nugent"). Claim 5 depends from claim 1 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Nugent merely describes detections by an ego/host vehicle of measurements directly of the obstacle itself and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 5 is therefore respectfully requested.
VI. Rejection of Claim 6 Under 35 U.S.C. # 103

Claim 6 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2010/0013615 ("Hebert"). Claim 6 depends from claim 1 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Hebert merely states that an ego/host vehicle can perform a guidance to avoid obstacles and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 6 is therefore respectfully requested.
VII. New Claims 14-17

Claims 14-17 have been added. Claims 14-17 do not add new matter and are supported by the present application, including the specification, as originally filed. Independent claim 14, from which claims 15-17 depend, includes features that the cited references do not disclose, and claims 14-17 are therefore allowable.
VIII. Conclusion

All issues raised having been addressed, it is therefore respectfully requested that the rejections be withdrawn. Prompt reconsideration and allowance of the present application are therefore earnestly solicited.
